idea.title: Homejoy: book a vetted home cleaner online in 60 seconds

source.text: Homejoy: book a vetted home cleaner online in 60 seconds, from $20 per hour, the platform takes a cut of each booking, launch country US. Score it as of 2012-07-01: use only evidence published on or before that date (set verdict.as_of). Founder: a seed-funded startup. Just go: do not ask questions. Use the slug homejoy.

idea.problem: Finding, vetting and booking a trustworthy home cleaner is slow and uncertain.
idea.customer: Busy urban households in US metros (assumed: young professionals in SF and NYC)
idea.solution: An online booking site: pick a time, get a vetted cleaner, pay online, in 60 seconds.
claims: book a vetted home cleaner online in 60 seconds
the platform takes a cut of each booking
assumptions: Scored as of 2012-07-01 with evidence published on or before that date
Seed round of roughly $1-2M, full-time team (not stated)
Launch metros SF Bay Area and NYC
Typical job 3 hours ($60); platform pays cleaners near the local mean wage
Take rate not stated; modelled from price minus cleaner pay

confidence.note: No 2012 source for client cleaning prices, cleaning-keyword CPC or rebooking rates; a dated price survey and CPC data would raise it.

gross_margin.note: $60 job − $45.60 SF cleaner pay − $2.04 Stripe = 20.6% of the booking (estimate). R5: costs kill shot holds it at 2.

ltv_cac.note: LTV $74 vs CAC ~$61 = 1.2 (estimate): thin, but repeat cleans could lift it.

pricing_power.note: Positioned as the cheapest: $20/h under Exec's $25/h. Competes on price, no premium.

build_effort.note: A booking page plus manual dispatch is weeks of work; the real build is cleaner ops.

skills_match.note: Seed-funded tech team assumed; field ops and labour-law skills not stated.

capital_needed.note: Seed covers a 1-city test; peers needed $3.3M-$24.5M to scale.

time_to_mvp.note: Landing page, Stripe and 10 cleaners can go live in 2-3 weeks (estimate).

sales_cycle.note: Consumer, same-day purchase of a $60 clean.

channel_readiness.note: Paid search and Groupon exist, costs unproven; no owned audience. Liquidity hit caps at 2.5.

search_demand.note: 877,980 maids employed in the US (BLS, May 2011): a mass, recurring need.

trend.note: Smartphones 35% to 46% of adults in a year; TaskRabbit at 9,000 tasks/month.

willingness_to_pay.note: People already pay Exec $25/h and agencies; demand is proven but price-sensitive.

free_alternatives.note: Craigslist, forums and word of mouth find cheap cleaners free; no vetting or booking.

competitor_density.note: TaskRabbit ($24.5M), Exec, Zaarly, Redbeacon (Home Depot), franchises. R5 ≤ 3.

differentiation.note: Lowest price + 60-second booking: easy to copy, no data or cost moat.

legal_regulatory.note: 1099 cleaners face the 2011 DOL/IRS misclassification push; CA AB 889 pending.

platform_dependency.note: Owns the site and customer data; paid channels have alternatives.

market_risk.note: Cleaning is a durable, recurring household need, not a fad.

skills.note: Startup skills assumed; no stated cleaning or marketplace ops track record.

assets.note: Seed capital; no audience, cleaner network or contracts stated.

interest.note: Founder motivation not stated; scored neutral.

sam.reasoning: TAM $3.5B × ~10% share for the SF Bay Area + NYC metros (dense, high-wage, high smartphone use)

competitor_price_range.value: $25/hour (Exec); TaskRabbit fee 13-30% on top of task price

price.reasoning: Founder's stated $20/hour × typical job of 3 hours (assumed) = $60

variable_cost_per_unit.reasoning: 3 h × $15.20 SF mean cleaner wage (BLS May 2011) = $45.60 + Stripe 2.9% × $60 + $0.30 = $2.04

gross_margin_pct.reasoning: ($60 − $47.64) ÷ $60 = 20.6% of booking value, before insurance, background checks and support

churn_monthly_pct.reasoning: 1 ÷ lifetime 2.77 months (6 jobs at 2.17 biweekly jobs/month)

expected_lifetime.reasoning: Assumed: an average customer books 6 cleans; no 2012 benchmark found

conversion_rate_pct.reasoning: Assumed half of Groupon first-time buyers book a second clean

cac.reasoning: Groupon: $60 clean sold at $30, Groupon keeps 50% → $15 in; cleaner paid $45.60 → $30.60 loss; ÷ 50% rebook = $61.20 per retained customer

fixed_costs_month.reasoning: Seed team of ~5 in SF at ~$8k/month each + $10k ops, insurance, tools

time_to_first_revenue_weeks.reasoning: 2 weeks to build a booking page and recruit 10 cleaners, 1 week to the first paid clean

verdict.launch_reason: Founder's stated launch country; SF and NYC have the highest cleaner wages and smartphone use.
verdict.cheapest_test: 7-day fake-door booking page for one SF zip cluster at $20 vs $28/hour, $1,000 of ads plus a deal, 10 vetted cleaners on call; measure bookings, contribution and 14-day rebooking.
kill_criteria: Fewer than 20 paid bookings from $1,000 of ads and deals by day 7 -> stop
Fewer than 30% of first-time customers rebook within 14 days -> stop
Contribution per job below $10 after cleaner pay and fees by day 7 -> raise price or stop
Fewer than 10 vetted cleaners willing to work at the offered pay by day 5 -> stop

rescue.change: Price at $25-30/hour on a recurring biweekly plan with the same insured cleaner, instead of 'cheapest from $20'
rescue.why: Fixes gross_margin and pricing_power (costs_eat_margin): contribution rises from ~$12 to ~$25 per job, and the plan gives a reason not to go direct
rescue.effort: 1-2 weeks: new pricing page and plan
rescue.requires: Retention data showing customers keep a $25+/h plan

rescue.change: Make cleaners W-2 employees (or a staffing partner's) in one city, sold as the only insured, employed-staff option
rescue.why: Defuses legal_platform_risk (2011 misclassification push, AB 889) and creates a real difference
rescue.requires: Employment counsel, workers' comp, a price that carries employer costs

rescue.change: Sell to employers as a perk (company accounts), like Exec's corporate offer
rescue.why: Fixes channel_readiness and CAC: one contract brings dozens of households

type_checks.note: Supply first: cleaners must be recruited and vetted before demand spend, and 75% annual turnover (up to 400%) means recruiting never stops.
Recurring same-cleaner jobs: at a 20% cut a weekly client pays ~$624/year in fees, a strong reason to go direct; agencies rely on non-hire clauses.

narrative.answer: **PIVOT**. Demand is huge and the tech easy, but at **$20/hour** the platform keeps about $12 a job after paying a Bay Area cleaner. Fund-raised rivals and the 2011 misclassification crackdown also squeeze it. Price up and win one city before scaling.
tldr: Mass, recurring need: **877,980** US maids (BLS, May 2011); smartphones at 46% of adults.
At $20/h, contribution is **~20%** of the booking after SF cleaner pay and Stripe; LTV:CAC ≈ 1.2.
TaskRabbit ($24.5M), Exec ($25/h) and Home Depot's Redbeacon are already there, and 1099 cleaners carry **legal risk**.

key_findings.title: $20/hour leaves almost nothing
key_findings.detail: A 3-hour $60 clean minus **$45.60** SF cleaner pay (BLS mean $15.20/h) and $2.04 Stripe leaves **$12.36**, 20.6% (estimate).

key_findings.title: Funded rivals already sell cleaning
key_findings.detail: TaskRabbit raised **$24.5M** and takes 13-30%; Exec charges $25/h and focuses on cleaning; Home Depot bought Redbeacon.

key_findings.title: Contractor cleaners face a 2011 crackdown
key_findings.detail: DOL and IRS signed a misclassification MOU on **2011-09-19**; California joined and AB 889 for housekeepers was pending.

narrative.recommendation: Run a 7-day SF test at $20 vs $28/hour with 10 vetted cleaners; only raise or spend more if **30%+** of first-time customers rebook and contribution exceeds $10 a job.
narrative.steelman: A **mass, recurring** need (877,980 maids) meets 46% smartphone adoption, and Exec's $25/h cleaning demand proves people book online. Whoever owns repeat cleaning in one dense city could build a frequent, high-LTV habit. The evidence backs demand; it does not back the $20 margin.

premortem.cause: Customers and cleaners go direct after a few cleans, so retained jobs per customer stay far below the 6 the model needs.
premortem.early_signal: Fewer than 30% of first-time customers rebook through the site within 14 days

premortem.cause: Discounted first cleans (deals, promo codes) cost more than repeat jobs earn back, burning the seed round.
premortem.early_signal: Contribution per job under $10, or CAC above $60 per retained customer, in the first 30 days

premortem.cause: A cleaner lawsuit or state ruling reclassifies 1099 cleaners as employees, adding payroll costs the $20 price can't carry.
premortem.early_signal: Cleaners asking about hours, overtime or W-2 status in the first 30 days

changes.what: Smartphone ownership rose from 35% to **46%** of US adults in about a year
Stripe launched: card payments by API at 2.9% + $0.30
TaskRabbit raised $17.8M to expand on-demand tasks to 5 cities
Exec launched $25/hour on-demand help in SF and raised $3.3M

why_now.note: The tools and the consumer habit arrived in 2011-12; the same window is open to funded rivals.

icp.who: Dual-income professionals in SF and NYC apartments with no time to clean, $75k+ household income
icp.pays_for_today: Exec at $25/hour, or an independent cleaner found by word of mouth (price unknown for 2012)
icp.trigger: Moving into a new apartment, a regular cleaner quits, or guests are coming

free_alternative.evidence: Searched Craigslist, forums, word of mouth: cleaners advertise free on neighbourhood forums (Brownstoner, 2010), but none vet or book; partial, not the whole job.

strong_competitor.evidence: TaskRabbit raised **$24.5M** (2011-12) with 2,000 Runners; Exec $3.3M at $25/h focused on cleaning; Zaarly $14.1M; Home Depot bought Redbeacon (2012-01).

graveyard.evidence: No closed online cleaning-booking company found before 2012-07; nearest is Kozmo, an on-demand local service that shut in 2001 (adjacent, not the same job).

no_distribution.evidence: Channels exist: deal sites (Groupon keeps ~50%), paid search (cleaning not among 2011's costliest CPCs), forums and employer perks; costly but credible.

costs_eat_margin.evidence: $60 clean − $45.60 SF cleaner pay (BLS May 2011) − $2.04 Stripe = **$12.36** (20.6%) before insurance and support (estimate).

weak_demand.evidence: Clear: 877,980 maids employed (BLS May 2011), TaskRabbit 9,000 tasks/month, smartphones up 11 points in a year.

legal_platform_risk.evidence: DOL-IRS misclassification MOU (2011-09-19), California joined, NY Domestic Workers' Bill of Rights (2010), CA AB 889 pending.

saturated_wave.evidence: About 1-4 look-alike launches (Exec, Zaarly NY, TaskRabbit expansion, Redbeacon) in the 12 months to 2012-07, far below 10.

customer.segment: Busy professionals in SF and NYC
customer.pain: Finding a trustworthy cleaner takes referrals, calls and vetting; paying one directly makes you a household employer
customer.today: Word of mouth, Craigslist, agencies, or Exec at $25/hour

use_cases.name: One-off deep clean before guests or a move
Recurring biweekly clean with the same cleaner

Win density in one city first

Recruit and vet 10 cleaners via job posts at $16-18/hour
Spend $1,000 on search ads and a forum or deal offer
Deliver the first cleans; collect ratings
Offer every customer a biweekly plan
